course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
review_basis: Source R2 Module 07 slides 45–49 independently audited; visual-first teaching narration, fresh audio only.
part_title: Async AI Tracing, Model Fallback and Quality Scorecards

scenes.title: Trace an Asynchronous AI Workflow
scenes.narration: This slide changes the pattern from synchronous to asynchronous processing. A client submits an AI job and receives a correlation identifier. The API places a message on SQS with that correlation ID and available trace context. A worker later polls the queue, extracts the identifiers and creates or continues an appropriately linked trace before invoking Bedrock. It stores the result in S3 and sends a completion notification containing the correlation ID. Follow the labels in the diagram: message attributes carry context across the queue boundary, worker spans record processing, and downstream calls record model invocation and storage. A correlation ID identifies the entire business job, even if several retries or separate traces occur. A trace ID and span context describe instrumented execution relationships. These should not be confused. Because an SQS message may be delivered more than once, the worker must process requests idempotently. To debug a missing result, search by correlation ID across the API, queue processing, model call, S3 write and notification. That connects asynchronous steps without assuming they form one uninterrupted HTTP request.

scenes.title: Observability for model fallback
scenes.narration: This slide compares three outcomes when a primary model might fail. Read the top flow: a user request reaches the primary model, which has a timeout limit. A bounded retry policy may try again with backoff. If the primary still fails, the application attempts a fallback model with its own timeout and compatibility rules. The first example trace shows primary success. The second shows a primary timeout followed by a successful fallback, giving the user a response but with greater total latency. The third shows both paths failing and a final error. The metric cards below distinguish primary success rate, fallback success rate, overall failure rate and tail latency. Those measurements prevent a misleading conclusion that the service is healthy just because fallback rescued many requests. A high fallback frequency can indicate a worsening primary dependency and increased costs. A fallback also needs prompt-format, model-permission and safety compatibility testing before production. Measure the user-visible latency, not just the successful invocation count. The operational goal is graceful degradation with clear evidence about which model served each response.

scenes.title: Cost and performance monitoring
scenes.narration: This dashboard combines throughput, token use, cache effectiveness, retrieval latency, model latency and estimated cost. Start with the top metrics. Token consumption and request count show how much work the application handles. Average model response time shows inference speed, while cache hit rate tells us how many repeated requests avoid expensive processing. Retrieval latency separately identifies time spent fetching context. The cost card estimates the financial result of all these choices. Below, the time-series charts show token usage, cost and the latency split through the day. The final row proposes practical optimizations: cache safe repeated answers, route simple tasks to smaller models, remove unnecessary prompt context, improve chunking and retrieval filters, and set budgets with alerts. Notice that each change has a possible quality trade-off. Shrinking context may lower cost but also remove evidence needed for grounding. Caching may be unsafe when users have different permissions or data freshness requirements. Monitor cost per successful, useful answer rather than lowering tokens at any price. The figures on the slide illustrate decisions, not guaranteed savings.

scenes.title: Quality and reliability scorecard
scenes.narration: This slide is a production scorecard for an AI assistant. Read each metric row across: definition, target or threshold, current result and status. Groundedness measures what proportion of claims have support from retrieved material. Citation coverage measures how often an answer points to its sources, which is related but not identical. Refusal accuracy checks whether the system correctly declines unsafe or out-of-scope requests. Error rate counts significant factual problems, and P ninety-five latency measures the slower tail of response times. Availability checks whether the service can reliably answer requests, while cost per successful response tracks economics. The current examples include groundedness around ninety-three percent, citation coverage around eighty-eight percent and a factual-error rate around four percent. These numbers do not all deserve the same status: some are healthy and others need attention. A scorecard should make weak dimensions visible rather than combining them into one flattering average. The acceptance limits are application-specific. A financial advice assistant may require much stricter controls than a casual content helper. Use clear definitions, reproducible samples and trend monitoring to support release and improvement decisions.

scenes.title: Operational runbook for poor AI answers
scenes.narration: This runbook starts when someone reports a wrong answer, such as an assistant claiming a thirty-day refund policy when the current policy is sixty days. Follow the steps along the top. First capture the problematic question, full answer and citations. Next, inspect the retrieved passages and their timestamps. In the slide, older policy files appear ahead of a newer document that contains the correct rule. Trace the request to see whether the retriever chose stale material or the model ignored good evidence. Then examine the prompt and model behavior, including whether the instructions require answers to be grounded in supplied documents. The solution may be to refresh the index, adjust filters and ranking, strengthen grounding instructions or change a model configuration. The final panel verifies that the new answer cites current policy and that regression tests still pass. Notice how the wrong answer isn't necessarily a hallucination created from nothing: it can be faithfully repeating outdated retrieved evidence. Diagnose ingestion freshness, retrieval relevance and generation separately. Record the incident and add the case to the evaluation set so future releases are tested against it.
